title: Past Questions: Module Two
lead: Every past question whose answerable parts are Module Two, filed by module rather than by year, most repeated first, with the course text assignments that drill the same diagrams.
intro:
Past questions only, and nothing else. This is your Question 2 practice, and it is the heavier of the two: Module Two is where the drawing marks are.

How to read the label above each question

Every question is here whole and as printed. The table above each one says, part by part, which module it belongs to and whether you answer it. The line under that names every other paper where the same thing was set.

Draw every diagram by hand. The ERD from a narrative has four sightings across the two papers, the DFD levels two, and reading a diagram back three. Those three between them are most of this module’s marks.

lockin.big: "ERD from a narrative, DFD in three levels, use case from a narrative, and reading a diagram back. Four things, asked over and over."
lockin.sub: Name every relationship with a verb, resolve a many to many with an associative entity, give cardinality AND ordinality, and write the balancing sentence under every levelled DFD.

questions.heading: The course text’s restaurant and car rental ERD assignments
questions.marks: Course text, Module Two Unit 4, pages 92 and 93

scenario.src: Course text, Module Two Unit 4, pages 92 and 93
scenario.tag: Course text, Module Two Unit 4, pages 92 and 93, a tutor marked assignment
scenario.text:
1. A restaurant wants to keep track of Customers and the Orders they place. A customer can place many orders, but each order belongs to one customer. Each order also contains one or more Menu Items, and a menu item can appear on many orders.
a. Identify all the entities involved.
b. List at least three attributes for each entity and mark the identifier.
c. Draw the complete ER diagram, showing all relationships and their cardinality
2. A car rental company wants to keep track of Customers and the Vehicles they rent. A customer can rent many vehicles over time, and a vehicle can be rented by many different customers over time, but never by more than one customer at once.
a. Identify all the entities involved, including any associative entity needed to record each individual rental.
b. List at least three attributes for each entity and mark the identifier for each.
c. Draw the ER diagram, stating the cardinality and ordinality of every relationship shown

breakdown.answer: The manual’s own version A restaurant wants to keep track of Customers and the Orders they place. A customer can place many orders, but each order belongs to one customer. Each order contains one or more Menu Items, and a menu item can appear on many orders. Identify the entities, list at least three attributes for each with the identifier marked, and draw the complete ER diagram showing all relationships and their cardinality.

exam.problem: Answer the assignment above in full in your book, then open this.
exam.answer:
Step 1: identify the entities. Three are named: Customer, Order, Menu Item. Singular nouns, each drawn as a rectangle.

Step 2: attributes, with the identifier marked.

CustomerOrderMenu Item
customer_id (identifier)
name
phone_number
address		order_id (identifier)
order_date
order_time
total_amount		item_code (identifier)
item_name
price
category

Step 3: name each relationship with a verb. Customer Places Order. Order Contains Menu Item.

Step 4: determine cardinality, asking each direction separately.

RelationshipQuestion oneQuestion twoResult
Customer Places OrderCan one customer place many orders? YesCan one order belong to many customers? No1:M
Order Contains Menu ItemCan one order contain many items? YesCan one item appear on many orders? YesM:N

Step 5: draw it. Three rectangles. A diamond labelled Places between Customer and Order, marked 1 on the Customer side and M on the Order side. A diamond labelled Contains between Order and Menu Item, marked M and N. Attribute ovals branching off each entity, identifiers marked.

The extra mark almost nobody takes

Add a sentence: the many-to-many between Order and Menu Item would be resolved by introducing an associative entity, Order Line, when the model is converted into database tables.

The car rental version of this assignment asks for that associative entity explicitly, which tells you the examiner cares about it.

The diagrams this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.

frames.teach: The ERD from a narrative is the most asked question in Module Two, and it is a five step procedure. Step one: underline every noun the organisation keeps data about. Each becomes a rectangle, named with a SINGULAR noun.
frames.ask: In the restaurant, which nouns are entities, and which noun is not?

frames.check: Customer, Order and Menu Item are entities. The restaurant itself is not, because the system keeps no data about it.
frames.teach: An entity always has more than one instance: one named customer is not an entity, Customer is. Step two: attributes. Give each entity three or four, and mark the identifier, the attribute that picks out one instance and which should never be blank and never need to change.
frames.ask: Step three names the relationships. What part of speech names a relationship, and what shape carries it in this course text?

frames.check: An active verb, in a diamond, because this text uses Chen notation.
frames.teach: Customer Places Order. Order Contains Menu Item. Written that way the diagram reads as a sentence, which is also how you answer the read-it-back questions.
frames.ask: Step four is cardinality. Ask each relationship in BOTH directions. Can one order contain many items, and can one item appear on many orders?

frames.check: Yes and yes, so it is many to many.
frames.teach: Yes and yes is M:N, and a many to many is resolved with an associative entity when the model is built. In the car rental question the examiner says it outright, "including any associative entity needed to record each individual rental": that sentence is telling you a many to many is hiding in the scenario.
frames.ask: Why can the rental not simply be an attribute of Customer or of Vehicle?

frames.check: Because the dates and the cost belong to the PAIRING, not to either one alone.
frames.teach: Introducing Rental turns one many to many into two one to many relationships, which is what makes the model buildable. Step five, and the part most answers drop: ordinality. Cardinality is the maximum, ordinality the minimum, optional at zero or mandatory at one.
frames.ask: A vehicle sits on the forecourt never yet rented. Mandatory or optional, and on which side?

frames.check: Optional, on the Vehicle side of the relationship to Rental.
frames.teach: And a Rental must have both a customer and a vehicle, so those sides are mandatory. Say both for every line, name your notation, and if the paper asks for Information Engineering or crow's foot instead, draw the fork on the many end and keep the same reasoning.

questions.heading: The course text’s sports centre use case assignment
questions.marks: Course text, Module Two Unit 2, pages 71 and 72

scenario.src: Course text, Module Two Unit 2, pages 71 and 72
scenario.tag: Course text, Module Two Unit 2, pages 71 and 72, a tutor marked assignment
scenario.text:
A sports centre offers facilities such as football pitches, tennis courts, basketball courts, and a gym. Customers can book these facilities for specific dates and time slots using an online booking system.
A Customer must first create an account and log in to the system. After logging in, the customer can view available sports facilities, check time slot availability, and make a booking for a preferred facility.
When making a booking, the system displays available time slots. The customer selects a suitable date and time, confirms the booking, and proceeds to make payment. Once payment is successful, the booking is confirmed and recorded in the system. The customer can also view, modify, or cancel bookings. The system sends a booking confirmation notification (via email or SMS) after a successful reservation.
A Staff/Admin manages the system by adding or updating facilities, setting availability schedules, and monitoring bookings. The admin can also generate reports on facility usage and customer bookings.
i. Create a use case diagram for the sports centre booking system in this scenario.
ii. Develop a use case narrative for ANY four use cases in the diagram

frames.teach: A use case diagram is four steps, and the course text numbers them, which means the examiner marks them: actors, use cases, association lines, then include and extend. Write the four as headings and answer under each.
frames.ask: Step one. Who are the actors here, and what rule names them?

frames.check: The Customer and the Staff or Admin, named with nouns.
frames.teach: The five questions that find actors: who provides input, who receives output, are interfaces required for other systems, are there events triggered automatically at a set time, and who maintains information in the system. Question three is the one that earns the extra mark here.
frames.ask: Payment is taken and a notification is sent. What does that make the payment company?

frames.check: An actor: an external server actor, because it responds to a request from the use case.
frames.teach: Four types, and the exam asks you to tell them apart: primary business actor benefits, primary system actor touches the keyboard, external server actor responds to a request, external receiver actor receives output without being primary.
frames.ask: Step two: what makes a phrase in the narrative a use case?

frames.check: It is something an actor DOES, written as a verb phrase.
frames.teach: Create Account, Log In, Check Availability, Make Booking, Make Payment, Cancel Booking, Add Facility, Generate Reports. Every one goes in an oval inside a boundary rectangle, and the actors stand outside it. An undrawn boundary loses marks on its own.
frames.ask: Two of those happen on every single booking. Which, and what relationship is that?

frames.check: Check Availability and Make Payment, and that is include.
frames.teach: Include is always, extend is sometimes. Both are dashed arrows, so the label and the direction are all you have, and the extend arrow points FROM the extension TO the base: "Cancel Booking extends Make Booking". Say it aloud and the arrow follows the sentence.
frames.ask: The second half asks for a narrative. Name as many of its seven parts as you can.

frames.check: Name and identifier, actors, description and goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions.
frames.teach: The part that separates a full answer is alternative flows, the failures: no slot free, payment declined, the slot taken while paying. The text praises use cases precisely because they surface exceptions and error handling, so writing three failure lines is writing the reason the technique exists.

questions.heading: 2024/2025, Question Three: the warehouse receiving stock

scenario.text: a. What are the elements of a Data Flow diagram? Enumerate any four (4) you know. (2 marks) b. Define what is meant by a data store in a process model. How should a data store be named? (1.5 marks) c. Read and interpret the Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) presented in Figure 1 by providing the cardinal relationships between the entities (3 marks) d. A warehouse has recently enforced a new management system to streamline the receiving process of stock. When truck drivers arrive, they are required to submit their trucks to the warehouse. On submission, the warehouse manager instructs the manual laborer to unload the trucks. It is important to note that a truck may or may not be carrying any stock. Once unloading is complete, the storekeeper is responsible for taking inventory of all available stock (spoilt, missing and in-good condition). The storekeeper then generates a comprehensive stock report, which is disseminated to the warehouse manager, the laborer involved in the unloading and the truck driver. Separately, both the truck drivers (regarding their delivery completion) and the labourers (regarding their unloading tasks) are required to submit individual activity reports directly to the manager. i. Draw an ERD to model the relationships between all identified entities. (5 marks) ii. Draw a Level 0 DFD to model the various processes involved. (4.5 marks) e. After drawing the Data flow diagrams for the above scenario, outline three (3) ways you can validate the integrity and correctness of the diagrams (1.5 marks)

breakdown.answer:
Asked Two recall parts (a, b), a diagram-reading part (c), a full ERD plus Level 0 DFD from the warehouse story (d), and diagram validation (e). Modules Three and Four.

Watch In d, the entities are TRUCK DRIVER, TRUCK, WAREHOUSE MANAGER, LABORER, STOREKEEPER, STOCK, STOCK REPORT, ACTIVITY REPORT. "A truck may or may not be carrying stock" is an optional relationship (zero or many).

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q3 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q3

a. DFD elements (2 marks)

External entity, process, data store, data flow.

b. Data store (1.5 marks)

A data store is data at rest in the system, a file or table where data is held between processes. It is named with a noun (for example D1 Stock), never a verb, and given a store number.

c. Reading Figure 1 (3 marks)

Read each relationship both ways from its crow's-foot marks. For example: one CUSTOMER makes many SALEs, and each SALE is made by one CUSTOMER (1:M); one CUSTOMER is targeted by many TARGETED PROMOTIONs, and each promotion targets many customers (M:N); a CUSTOMER adds many CUSTOMER FAVORITEs (1:M); an AVAILABLE TUNE is included in many CUSTOMER INTERESTs (M:N). State the cardinality (one or many, optional or mandatory) for each line the figure draws.

Answer, continued

d. Warehouse ERD and Level 0 DFD (9.5 marks)

ERD: entities TRUCK DRIVER, TRUCK, MANAGER, LABORER, STOREKEEPER, STOCK, STOCK REPORT, ACTIVITY REPORT. A TRUCK DRIVER submits many TRUCKs; a TRUCK may carry zero or many STOCK (optional); a LABORER unloads many TRUCKs; a STOREKEEPER takes inventory of STOCK and generates STOCK REPORTs; drivers and labourers submit ACTIVITY REPORTs to the MANAGER. Crow's foot throughout, with the optional (circle) mark on the truck-to-stock line.

Level 0 DFD: external entities TRUCK DRIVER and MANAGER; processes 1.0 Receive and unload truck, 2.0 Take inventory, 3.0 Generate stock report, 4.0 Submit activity report; data stores D1 Stock and D2 Reports. Wire the flows so each process has input and output, and balance them against the context diagram.

e. Validate the diagrams (1.5 marks)

Check every process has both an input and an output (no black holes or miracles); check no illegal flow (every flow touches a process); and check the levels balance (the flows in and out of a process match its explosion).

The diagram this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.

frames.teach: A DFD answers one question: what does the system DO with data. Four symbols carry the whole notation, and the naming rules are marks on their own.
frames.ask: Name the four elements and the shape of each, before the answer does.

frames.check: External agent, a rectangle. Data flow, an arrow. Process, a rounded rectangle. Data store, an open ended rectangle.
frames.teach: Naming: an agent is a singular noun, a flow is named with nouns, a process must be a verb and must not be procedural, and a data store takes a noun with no verbs. The text's own bad example is "Add 1 to the counter", which should be "Increment counter".
frames.ask: In this warehouse, the truck driver, the manager, the labourer and the storekeeper are all named. Which of them are external agents?

frames.check: The truck driver. The manager, labourer and storekeeper work inside the system, so their work is the processes.
frames.teach: That judgement decides whether your diagram is clean or crowded. Anyone whose work the system records is INSIDE it; anyone who hands something in or takes something out is outside. Reports going to the manager are then flows from a process to an agent only if he is treated as a recipient, and the question says the report is disseminated to him, so he is.
frames.ask: Now the levels. What is on a context diagram that is not on a Level 0, and the other way round?

frames.check: Context has the whole system as one process and usually no data stores. Level 0 has the major processes AND the stores.
frames.teach: And there is exactly one Level 0 per system, which is asked directly. A Level 1 explodes ONE process from Level 0, never the whole diagram.
frames.ask: Part (e) asks for three ways to validate your diagrams. One of them is the single most examined DFD rule. Which?

frames.check: Balancing: the inputs and outputs of a process are conserved when it is decomposed.
frames.teach: The other two: check every process for the three errors, black hole with no outputs, miracle with no inputs, gray hole whose inputs cannot produce its outputs; and check every flow touches a process, which rules out store to store, agent to agent and store to agent.
frames.ask: Part (b) asks how a data store should be named. What is the rule, and what is the phrase that separates a store from a flow?

frames.check: A noun, avoiding verbs and physical descriptions. A store is data at rest; a flow is data in motion.
frames.teach: Write that sentence into the answer: it is one line and it proves you know the difference the examiner is testing. Then, for part (d), draw the ERD first and the Level 0 second: the nouns you find for the ERD are the stores you will need for the DFD, so the two halves feed each other.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question One: the landlord and the estate agent

scenario.text: A landlord owns one of many houses and asks the only estate agent he knows to help find a suitable tenant. The agent (who manages many houses) contacts his supervisor to inform him about the availability of the house. The supervisor indicates interest and agrees to rent the house. After the agreement, the supervisor moves into the house with the help of the agent. Before occupation, they both clean the house. Once settled, the supervisor occupies the house and pays rent through the agent, who then forwards the payment to the landlord. a. Draw an ERD to model the relationships between the identified entities (4.5 mks) b. Data Flow Diagram (DFD): i. Draw a Context diagram to model the entire system (1.5 mks) ii. Draw a Level 0 DFD to show various processes involved (4.5 mks) iii. Draw a Level 1 DFD to model the process of rent payment (3 mks) c. The resulting system is successful when it is acceptable to the customer and it will fail if it cannot establish upper-management commitment to the project. Enumerate (3) other reasons a project will succeed and (3) other reasons it can fail (3 mks) d. Read and interpret the following (using forward and backward chaining) (1 mk)

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given A landlord, an estate agent, a supervisor (the tenant), houses, and rent payments that flow supervisor to agent to landlord.

Asked Four separate things: an ERD (a), three DFDs (b), reasons a project succeeds and fails (c), and reading a printed ERD fragment (d). Parts a, b and d test Modules Three and Four; part c tests Module Six.

Marks 17.5 in all. Part b is worth the most (9), so the three DFDs deserve the most time and care.

Watch The examiner asks the ERD in no particular notation, so use the crow's foot. In the DFDs, keep every flow touching a process, and make the three levels balance.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 25/26 Q1 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 25/26 Q1

a. Entity-relationship diagram (4.5 marks)

The nouns kept as records are LANDLORD, HOUSE, AGENT, SUPERVISOR (the tenant) and PAYMENT. The relationships from the story: a landlord owns many houses; an agent manages many houses; an agent serves a supervisor; a supervisor occupies a house; a supervisor makes payments; an agent forwards payments to the landlord.

Answer, continued

b. Data flow diagrams (9 marks)

Context diagram: one process "0 Rental system" in the middle, with SUPERVISOR and LANDLORD as external entities. Flows: supervisor sends "house request" and "rent payment" in; the system sends "house availability" back to the supervisor and "forwarded payment" to the landlord. No data stores at this level (draw it exactly as Figure 3.2 in Module Three, with these labels).

Level 0: explode process 0 into the major processes: 1.0 Match tenant to house, 2.0 Agree and clean, 3.0 Collect and forward rent. Add data stores D1 Houses and D2 Payments. Wire the flows so each process has an input and an output, and so the "house request" in and "forwarded payment" out still match the context diagram (balance).

Level 1 of process 3.0 (rent payment): explode 3.0 into 3.1 Receive payment from supervisor, 3.2 Record payment (to D2 Payments), 3.3 Forward payment to landlord. The total flows in and out (payment in, forwarded payment out) balance process 3.0.

Answer, continued

c. Three more reasons to succeed and three to fail (3 marks)

Succeed (besides customer acceptance): clear and agreed requirements; strong user involvement throughout; a realistic schedule and budget with good project management.

Fail (besides lack of upper-management commitment): unclear or constantly changing requirements; little or no user involvement; poor planning, estimation or testing.

d. Reading the fragment (1 mark)

The bar at the Customer end means "one" and the circle-with-crow's-foot at the Order end means "zero or many". So, forward chaining: one CUSTOMER places zero or many ORDERs. Backward chaining: each ORDER is placed by one and only one CUSTOMER.

The diagrams this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.

frames.teach: This question is the heaviest drawing question on either paper: an ERD, three DFD levels, a list question and a read-it-back. Take them in the order printed, and keep the same entity names throughout so the examiner can follow you.
frames.ask: In the narrative, who or what are the entities? Watch the trap in the word supervisor.

frames.check: Landlord, House, Agent, Supervisor, and Payment or Rent.
frames.teach: The supervisor is the TENANT in this story, which the wording hides. Read the whole narrative once before naming anything: the relationships, owns, manages, rents, pays, forwards, are the verbs your diamonds will carry.
frames.ask: The landlord owns one of many houses, and the agent manages many houses. What cardinalities does that give you?

frames.check: Landlord owns houses, one to many. Agent manages houses, one to many.
frames.teach: Quote the phrase beside each one: "owns one of many houses", "who manages many houses". A cardinality justified by the examiner's own words cannot be argued with.
frames.ask: Now part (b), three diagrams. What sits on the context diagram for this system?

frames.check: One process, the whole lettings system, with the Landlord, the Agent and the Supervisor around it.
frames.teach: Then Level 0: the major processes, numbered, with the stores, and there is exactly one of these. Then Level 1, exploding the rent payment process only, which is what part (b)(iii) names.
frames.ask: Before you hand it in, what one sentence do you write under the Level 1 diagram?

frames.check: That the diagrams balance: the flows in and out of the parent are all accounted for among the children.
frames.teach: Ten seconds, one mark, every time. Part (c) then leaves diagrams behind: three more reasons a project succeeds and three why it fails. Answer from the text's nine principles, which is the nearest thing it has to a list of success factors: user involvement, a problem solving approach, phases and activities, standards, justification as a capital investment, willingness to cancel or revise scope, divide and conquer, design for growth and change, and proper planning and project management.
frames.ask: Part (d) prints a small diagram and asks you to read it forwards and backwards. What does reading it backwards mean?

frames.check: Stating the same relationship from the other entity's point of view.
frames.teach: "One Customer places many Orders" forwards, "each Order is placed by exactly one Customer" backwards. Read every line of a given ERD both ways and you have answered any read-it-back question, in this paper and in 2024/2025 Q3(c) and Q4(b).

questions.heading: 2024/2025, Question Four: process and data modelling, end to end

scenario.text: a. As a system analyst, you have been asked to draw a Data Flow diagram to explain the processes involved in food ordering at a Nigerian airport. Outline any four (4) reasons it is helpful to first Model the processes. (2 marks) b. i) Using appropriate diagrammatic illustrations, explain the various cardinal relationship in ERD (use Information Engineering style) (3 marks) ii) What makes a relationship optional? With a diagram, give a practical illustration. (1.5 marks) iii) What does the term 'Data Balancing' mean? (1 mark) c. In a tabular form, outline three major differences between Process Modelling and Data Modelling (1.5 marks) d. You are to develop a sales management system that allows sales representative to record orders placed by customers, checkout orders, and also allows the store keeper to keep inventory of product in the warehouse. A customer can place more than one order however each order must be placed by one customer. Each sales representative serves zero to many customers per time, however each customer is served by only one sales representative. Each order contains one or more products and zero or more products are stores in only one warehouse. Draw an entity relationship diagram for this scenario. (3 marks) e. 'Data cannot move between entities in a Data flow diagram.' Explain this sentence with an appropriate diagrammatic example. (1 mark) f. We wish to collect information about researchers, their institutions and research interests and then design a database that will track their activities. Draw an ERD to model the relationships between identified entities. [Hint: Each researcher is associated with only one institution and each researcher has several research interests]. (3 marks) g. You are designing a hospital management system for a client who has given you a short time frame of just one month. Which system acquisition strategy do you choose? Enumerate any three factors that supports your choice. (1.5 marks)

6 of 7 parts are yours.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q4 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q4

a. Four reasons to model (2 marks)

A model is a clear picture non-technical users can check; it separates what the system does from how it is built; it shows the system boundary and everything it touches; and it breaks a large system into manageable processes.

b. Cardinality, optionality, data balancing (5.5 marks)

i. In crow's foot: one-to-one (a bar at each end), one-to-many (a bar at one end, a crow's foot at the other), many-to-many (a crow's foot at each end); draw each on a line between two entity rectangles. ii. A relationship is optional when the minimum is zero, drawn with a circle on the line (a customer may have zero orders). iii. Data balancing means the data flowing into and out of a process on a parent diagram must match the data flowing into and out of its child diagram when it is exploded.

c. Process modelling versus data modelling (1.5 marks)

Process modelling (DFD)Data modelling (ERD)
Shows data in motionShows data at rest
Built from processes and flowsBuilt from entities and relationships
Answers how data movesAnswers what data is stored
Answer, continued

d. Sales management ERD (3 marks)

Entities SALES REP, CUSTOMER, ORDER, PRODUCT, WAREHOUSE. SALES REP serves zero-or-many CUSTOMERs, each CUSTOMER served by one rep; CUSTOMER places one-or-many ORDERs, each ORDER by one customer; ORDER contains one-or-many PRODUCTs; WAREHOUSE stores zero-or-many PRODUCTs. Mark the optional (circle) and many (crow's foot) ends as the words say.

e. Data cannot move between entities (1 mark)

A data flow must touch a process at one end, so you cannot draw an arrow straight from one external entity rectangle to another: put a process bubble between them. For example, Customer to Bank is wrong; Customer to "1.0 Process payment" to Bank is right.

f. Researcher ERD (3 marks)

Entities RESEARCHER, INSTITUTION, RESEARCH INTEREST. A RESEARCHER belongs to one INSTITUTION (many researchers per institution, so INSTITUTION 1:M RESEARCHER); a RESEARCHER has many RESEARCH INTERESTs (1:M, or M:N if interests are shared). Crow's foot with the one bar at the institution end.

g. Acquisition strategy (1.5 marks)

With only one month, buy a packaged solution or outsource, not build. Factors: the very short time available, the lack of in-house build capacity in the time, and that a hospital admin system is not so unique that a package cannot fit.

The diagrams this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.

Give three cogent reasons for your decision as Project Manager. (3 Marks)

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q1 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q1

a. Two elicitation techniques (4 marks)

Interview the head librarian: suitable because they hold the borrowing rules and can be probed in depth; advantage, rich detailed information; limitation, slow and only a few people. Questionnaire to student borrowers: suitable because it cheaply reaches the large, scattered student body; advantage, wide reach at low cost; limitation, no follow-up and often a low response rate.

b. Requirements and a reason (6.5 marks)

Functional: the system shall let a member borrow a book; shall let a member reserve a book; shall calculate and record fines. Non-functional: the system shall respond within two seconds; shall be available 99.9% of the time; shall keep member data secure. Reason for multiple levels: different levels (a student, a librarian, a head of library) use the system differently, so gathering from all of them captures needs that a single level would miss.

c. Methodology and scope creep (7 marks)

i. Unclear requirements call for an adaptive method: choose prototyping or RAD, which discover requirements as they go. Map the phases: plan, then build a prototype, review it with the client, refine, and repeat until the requirements settle, then implement and support. ii. Refuse (or defer) the new features, because they threaten the agreed schedule and budget, they risk the quality of the nearly finished system, and they should be handled as a change request or a later release.

frames.teach: Requirements questions have a house style, and it is the same on both papers: name the technique, then say who you would use it on, what it collects, why it suits this project, and one limitation. Four short clauses each.
frames.ask: Name the seven fact finding techniques before the answer lists them.

frames.check: Sampling documentation, research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping, and joint requirements planning.
frames.teach: For a library system, the cheapest information is already written down: sampling the existing documentation, the accession registers, the loan slips and the overdue reports, which shows the real business rules and the data quality problems without costing a librarian a minute.
frames.ask: Which technique would you pair with it, given you must reach students, librarians and management?

frames.check: Questionnaires for the many, interviews for the few.
frames.teach: Questionnaires collect from many respondents quickly and cheaply, in two formats: free format, where the respondent writes, and fixed format, where they choose, in multiple choice, rating or ranking. Interviews are the expensive one, so reserve them and prepare an interview guide.
frames.ask: Part (b) wants functional and non functional requirements. What separates the two?

frames.check: Functional says what the system must DO; non functional says how well it must do it.
frames.teach: Functional for a library: issue a loan, reserve a title, calculate a fine, produce an overdue list. Non functional: respond within two seconds, be available during opening hours, keep borrower data private, run on the existing hardware. Write them as numbered one liners, never as a paragraph.
frames.ask: 2025/2026 Q5 adds three more categories: business, user and system requirements. What is the difference between a business requirement and a functional one?

frames.check: A business requirement is the outcome the organisation wants; a functional requirement is a thing the system does to deliver it.
frames.teach: So: business, cut the time to find a title; user, a student can search the catalogue from a phone; functional, the system searches by title, author and subject; non functional, results in under two seconds; system, it runs on the existing web server and integrates with the student register. One line each, five labels, five marks.
frames.ask: Part (b)(iii) asks why elicitation should involve users from different organisational levels. One sentence?

frames.check: Because each level sees a different system, so asking only one level produces requirements that are incomplete or contradictory.
frames.teach: Management sees cost and control, supervisors see the workflow, clerks see the screen they use all day. The text's own reason is that people are the source of requirements information, and conflicting requirements have to be found and resolved before they are built.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Six: the AI programming platform

scenario.text: A private university wants to build an AI-supported programming learning platform for undergraduate students. The system should help students learn Python, Java, and C++ by providing coding exercises, automated feedback, debugging support, lecturer dashboards, plagiarism alerts, and adaptive learning recommendations. The university expects the system to support 8,000 students across three campuses. At the start of the project, requirements are unclear. Students want instant answers to coding problems, lecturers want the system to promote independent thinking rather than answer copying, administrators want analytics on student performance, and the ICT unit is concerned about security, scalability, integration with the learning management system, and maintenance cost. Halfway through the project, university management requests additional features: AI-generated lecture notes, automatic grading of essays, and integration with the university payment portal. a. Identify the weaknesses of the as-is system, the expected improvements in the to-be system, and the assumptions that must be validated before development begins. (3.5 mks). b. Design a requirements elicitation plan for the system using at least four techniques. For each technique, identify the stakeholders involved, the type of information to be collected, and why the technique is suitable for this project. (4 mks). c. Write short notes on: Unified Modeling Language (UML) (also state the inventors and its uses). (2 mks) d. Categories UML diagrams into two broad categories. Mention two diagrams in each of the categories and describe it function (4 mks) e. With the aid of diagrams, explain the following class relationships in system analysis: (i) Inheritance, (ii) Composition, (iii) Aggregation, and (iv) Association. (4 mks)

The elicitation plan in part (b) is the same family as 2024/2025 Q1(a). Parts (c), (d) and (e) are UML and class relationships, which is Module Three: skip them in the hall, but they are worth reading, because the objective half draws on all three modules.

(b)Module TwoAnswer itAn elicitation plan with four techniques, their stakeholders and what each collects

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 25/26 Q6 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 25/26 Q6

a. As-is, to-be and assumptions (3.5 marks)

As-is weaknesses: no single platform, so learning is unsupported; no automated feedback or plagiarism checking; no analytics for administrators. To-be improvements: one platform teaching three languages with automated feedback, debugging support, plagiarism alerts and analytics. Assumptions to validate: that 8,000 students across three campuses have reliable network access; that the platform can integrate with the existing learning management system; that the AI feedback is accurate enough to be trusted.

b. Elicitation plan (4 marks)

  • Interview lecturers: information on the learning outcomes and marking rules; suitable because they hold the academic requirements and can be probed in depth.
  • Questionnaire to students: information on what help they want; suitable because it cheaply reaches 8,000 scattered students.
  • Observation of a lab session: information on how students really code and get stuck; suitable because it shows real behaviour.
  • Document review of the learning management system: information on existing data and integration points; suitable because it grounds the design in what exists.

c. Short notes on UML (2 marks)

UML is a standard set of diagram notations for modelling object-oriented systems, created by Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson. Its uses: to visualise, specify, construct and document a software system in one shared language.

d. Two categories of UML diagram (4 marks)

Structural diagrams model what the system is: the class diagram (classes and relationships) and the object diagram (objects at a moment). Behavioural diagrams model what it does: the use case diagram (what users can do) and the activity diagram (a process flow); the sequence diagram is another.

e. Four class relationships (4 marks)

Inheritance (hollow triangle, is-a): a Postgraduate is a Student. Composition (filled diamond, life-or-death has-a): an Order is made of Order Lines. Aggregation (hollow diamond, loose has-a): a Department has Lecturers who survive it. Association (plain line): a Doctor treats a Patient. Draw the four side by side as Figure 5.2 in Module Five.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q6 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q6

a. The analyst as problem solver (5.5 marks)

The analyst studies a business to find where it loses time, money or accuracy, works out whether technology can help, and specifies the system that solves the problem. The solution is usually an information system, but not always. The analyst researches and understands the problem, verifies the benefit outweighs the cost, defines requirements, develops alternatives, recommends the best, details it, implements and monitors, which is exactly a problem-solving sequence. That is why the analyst is a business problem solver and the bridge between users and the technical team.

b. Use case and activity diagrams (12 marks)

Use case (i): actor PATIENT; use cases Make appointment, Change appointment, Cancel appointment, Add patient. "Make appointment" includes "Check patient and bills". Draw it as Figure 2.1 in Module Two with these labels.

Activity (ii): start, "Receive call", decision "current patient?" (no leads to "Add patient" then continue), decision "unpaid bills?" (yes leads to "Forward to accounts" then end), then decision "change or cancel?": if so "Find and cancel appointment"; otherwise "Match desired times to available dates" and "Schedule appointment"; end. Draw it as Figure 5.3.

The diagram this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Two: the hospital patient billing system

scenario.text: A patient visits a hospital to use the patient billing system in order to make enquiries about the types of drugs he can buy. On confirmation, the doctor advises the patient on which drugs to use for his condition. Note that a patient must be assigned to only one doctor but a doctor can have many patients. A patient can have only one insurance ID to prevent insurance fraud. a. Draw a class diagram for this scenario. [Hint: Show multiplicity where necessary] (5 mks) b. Draw a use case diagram for the system. (5 mks) c. Draw an activity diagram to show the system's process flow. (5 mks) d. State three (3) drawbacks of multiple inheritance. (2.5 mks)

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 25/26 Q2 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 25/26 Q2

a. Class diagram (5 marks)

Four classes: PATIENT, NURSE, DOCTOR, INSURANCE. Give each attributes and a method. The rules give the multiplicities: a DOCTOR treats many PATIENTs but each PATIENT has one DOCTOR (1 to *); a PATIENT has one INSURANCE and an insurance covers one patient (1 to 1); a NURSE attends many PATIENTs (1 to *).

b. Use case diagram (5 marks)

Actors: PATIENT, NURSE, DOCTOR, INSURANCE CARRIER. Use cases inside the boundary: Make enquiry, Check vitals, Refer to doctor, Confirm insurance, Advise on drugs. "Attend patient" includes "Check insurance" (it must always happen, since he will not be attended without insurance). Draw it as Figure 2.1 in Module Two with these labels.

c. Activity diagram (5 marks)

Start, then action "Patient makes enquiry", then a decision "has insurance?": the "no" branch ends (not attended); the "yes" branch flows to "Nurse checks vitals", "Refer to doctor", "Doctor confirms insurance with carrier", "Advise on drugs", then end. Draw it as Figure 5.3 with this flow.

d. Drawbacks of multiple inheritance (2.5 marks)

The diamond problem (ambiguity when two parents give the same method); increased complexity of the class hierarchy; and name clashes between members inherited from different parents.

The diagram this question asks for, drawn. Copy the shape, not the wording: the entity names and the cardinalities are what carry the marks.
